questions.prompt: How does an iterator signal that it has no more items?
questions.explanation: `__next__` raises `StopIteration` when it's exhausted. `for` loops, `list()` and other consumers catch it and stop.

sources.claim: An iterator's `__next__()` returns the next item and raises StopIteration when there are no further items.

questions.prompt: After `it = iter([1, 2])`, you call `list(it)` twice. What does the second call return?
questions.explanation: An iterator can only be consumed once. The first `list()` exhausts it, so the second gets nothing. A list is an iterable: each `iter()` call on it creates a fresh iterator.

sources.title: Glossary — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: A list produces a fresh iterator on each `iter()` call, whereas iterating an iterator again just returns the same exhausted object, which yields nothing more.

sources.title: Built-in Types — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Once an iterator's `__next__()` has raised StopIteration it must keep raising it on later calls.

questions.prompt: Given `def gen(): print('start'); yield 1`, what does `g = gen()` print?
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function only creates a generator object. The body starts running on the first `next()` and pauses at each `yield`.

sources.claim: Calling a generator function returns an iterator; the body executes only when that iterator's `__next__()` is called, running until a `yield`.

questions.prompt: Explain how a generator function differs from a normal function, and why that suits streaming LLM tokens to a client.

model_answer.summary: Calling a generator returns an object that runs the body lazily, pausing at each `yield` and keeping its local state. Values are produced one at a time, so tokens can be forwarded as they arrive.
key_points: Calling a generator function returns a generator object without running the body
The body runs until a `yield`, hands back a value, then pauses with its local state kept
It resumes on the next `next()` call, producing values lazily, on demand
Memory use stays constant, and the consumer can forward each token to the client as it arrives instead of waiting for the whole response

questions.explanation: Streaming APIs, including LLM SDKs and FastAPI's `StreamingResponse`, are built on this pattern: the producer yields chunks and the consumer handles each one straight away.

questions.prompt: Why is `sum(x * x for x in range(10**8))` safer than `sum([x * x for x in range(10**8)])`?

choices.text: The generator expression produces values one at a time, so memory use stays constant
List comprehensions cannot be passed to `sum`

questions.explanation: The list comprehension builds all 100 million results in memory before `sum` starts. The generator expression hands `sum` one value at a time.

sources.claim: A generator expression evaluates its elements lazily, only when the iterator is asked for a value, while a list display builds a new list object.

questions.prompt: Which of these is evaluated lazily?
questions.explanation: Parentheses make a generator expression, which yields items on demand. List and set comprehensions, and `sorted`, build the whole collection straight away.

sources.title: 6. Expressions — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Generator expressions (in parentheses) are evaluated lazily as the iterator is asked for values, whereas list and set displays and comprehensions build the full collection.

questions.prompt: Describe a generator pipeline that counts error lines in a very large JSONL log file without loading the file into memory. Why does it stay memory-safe?

model_answer.summary: Chain generators: iterate the file line by line, parse each line, filter for errors, and count as you go. Only one line is in memory at a time.
key_points: Iterate over the open file object, which reads one line at a time
A generator parses each line with `json.loads` and yields the record
A generator expression, or a filter step, keeps only records whose level is error
`sum(1 for _ in errors)` counts them; every stage is lazy, so only one line is held in memory at once

questions.explanation: Composable lazy stages are how you process traces, logs and datasets far larger than RAM. The same shape works for processing agent traces in week 7.

questions.prompt: What does `yield from inner()` do inside a generator?

choices.text: Yields the `inner` generator object as one value
Delegates to `inner`, yielding each of its values and passing `send()` and `throw()` through

questions.explanation: `yield from` hands control to the sub-generator until it finishes, forwarding every value it yields plus any `send()` or `throw()` calls. It also evaluates to the sub-generator's return value.

sources.title: 6. Expressions — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: `yield from` passes the sub-iterator's values straight to the caller, forwards `send()` and `throw()` to it, and evaluates to its StopIteration value (the return value).

sources.title: PEP 380 – Syntax for Delegating to a Subgenerator | peps.python.org
sources.claim: PEP 380 defines `yield from` as delegation to a subgenerator, forwarding yielded values, sent values and thrown exceptions, and using its return value as the expression's value.

questions.prompt: What does `list(g())` return when `def g(): yield from range(3); yield 'done'`?
questions.explanation: `yield from range(3)` yields 0, 1 and 2 as separate values, and then the generator yields `'done'`.

sources.claim: With `yield from`, each value produced by the underlying iterable is passed directly to the caller as a separate item.

questions.prompt:
```python
def stream():
    print("start")
    yield "Hel"
    yield "lo"

g = stream()
```
Which of these are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `g = stream()` prints nothing: the body hasn't started yet
Calling `stream()` runs the whole body and stores both values
Each `next(g)` restarts the body, printing `start` again
Between `next` calls the generator keeps its local state

questions.explanation: Calling a generator function returns a generator iterator without running the body (a, so b is wrong). Each `next()` runs the body until the next `yield`: the first prints `start` and returns `"Hel"` (c). At a `yield` the generator suspends, keeping its local variables, and resumes where it left off (e) rather than starting fresh (d). That is why a generator can forward streamed tokens one at a time.

sources.title: 3. Data model
sources.claim: A generator function, when called, returns an iterator; calling its `__next__()` method executes the body until it provides a value with a yield expression.

sources.title: Glossary
sources.claim: Each `yield` temporarily suspends a generator iterator, remembering its execution state including local variables, and on resuming it picks up where it left off, unlike functions, which start fresh on every call.

questions.prompt:
```python
with open("app.jsonl") as f:
    records = (json.loads(line) for line in f)
    errors = (r for r in records if r["level"] == "error")
    n = sum(1 for _ in errors)
```
Which of these are true for a very large log file? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Looping over `f` reads the file one line at a time
`records` parses every line as soon as it is defined
Lines are parsed only as `sum` pulls items through
Using `f.readlines()` instead uses the same memory
Only the current line is held in memory at a time

questions.explanation: Looping over a file object reads it line by line, which is memory efficient (a). Generator expressions are lazy: apart from the outermost iterable (here just the file object), nothing is evaluated until values are requested, so `records` parses nothing when defined (b) and each line is parsed only as `sum` pulls it through (c). So only the current line is in memory (e). `f.readlines()` builds a list of every line first, so memory grows with the file (d).

sources.title: 7. Input and Output
sources.claim: Looping over a file object to read lines is memory efficient, fast and simple; `list(f)` or `f.readlines()` reads all the lines of a file into a list.

sources.title: 6. Expressions
sources.claim: In a generator expression, all expressions except the outermost iterable are evaluated lazily, when values are requested from the generator.
